newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Greek troops celebrate Orthodox Easter in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Greek troops celebrate Orthodox Easter in Albania.

text.p: Greek troops sent to Albania to guard aid deliveries celebrated Orthodox Easter on Sunday in the ruins of a military camp razed during the unrest that swept the Balkan nation last month.
The 400 Greek soldiers at Yzberish, part of an eight-nation United Nations-approved force of 6,000 sent to Albania, roasted lambs on spits and listened to traditional music as they celebrated Easter.

"It is just like an Easter at home until you look up," said second lieutenant Cristos Kaliptsidis, pointing to the groups of inquisitive Albanians watching the celebrations from surrounding vantage points.

The Greek troops were living in tents alongside army huts blown apart by grenades and gutted by fire in the rampage as Albanians angered by the loss of savings in fraudulent pyramid schemes looted military arsenals.
"In this country there is no war, no bombs but so many buildings have been destroyed it looks like a war zone," Kaliptsidis said.

The largest ceremony for the orthodox minority in mainly-Moslem Albania was delayed for eight hours because of a dusk-to-dawn curfew imposed across the Balkan nation following the unrest in February and March.
Thousands clutching lit candles for what should have been a midnight service gathered at the main orthodox church in Tirana under the watchful eye of police toting Kalashnikovs.

"Within the turmoil of the last months in Albania, several dark powers have been released, causing unbelieveable destruction. Reconciliation is an urgent need," Albania's orthodox primate Archbishop Anastassios told the congregation of about 5,000.
Over 300 people have been killed and more than 700 injured in the recent violence. But the situation has calmed since the arrival 10 days ago of the multinational security force.
Young and old alike gathered to hear the archbishop's homily then wind their way down a narrow alley, lined with beggars, into the ornate church to light candles to commemorate the dead.

Until the fall of communism in late 1990, the church had been boarded up, closed by dictator Enver Hoxha who banned all religious practices for 23 of the 46 years that Albania was isolated under hardline Stalinist rule.
Regular attendees said the numbers celebrating Easter have risen annually since 1990 but this year there were nearly three times as many as last year.
"People think coming here will bring us closer together," regular churchgoer Anastasia Taci told Reuters.
"Usually this ceremony is at night and it is much better but at least we are still celebrating despite all the trouble."
Taci joined the rest of the crowd as they cracked open and ate red-painted hardboiled eggs, a symbol of friendship.
"We used to eat these red eggs when Hoxha ruled but in secret," Taci said in a quiet voice. "What you feel in your spirit no one can take away from you."
The archbishop called on members of Albania's orthodox church, who account for about 20 percent of the country's 3.4 million people, to put the crisis behind them.
Armed rebels, who blame President Sali Berisha for the pyramids disaster, still control much of southern Albania and police daily report further shootings and explosions.

"It is time we stopped thinking of the old ideologies and of the new ideals," said the archbishop, speaking from a makeshift stage and surrounded by choirboys clad in bright orange that contrasted with the peeling, dilapidated buildings.
"Brothers, let us forgive everyone in this day of reconciliation."
